title: Listing every outcome
objectives: List a sample space and pick out an event inside it.
Keep outcomes apart when order makes them different.

screens.prose: Roll two fair dice, one red and one blue. Each cell is one result: the row is the red die, the column is the blue die. You met this grid in the counting course.
screens.question: Shade every result where the total is 7.

hints.text: If the red die shows 1, what must the blue die show?
The sevens run along one diagonal, starting at the top right.
Red 1 needs blue 6, red 2 needs blue 5, and so on up to red 6. That is one cell in every row.

feedback.correct: Six of the 36 results add to 7, one in every row.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try every red result from 1 to 6, and check that each shaded pair adds to 7.

screens.prose: Now toss a coin three times. Each path from the start to the end is one full result, such as HTH. Tap a path to select it.
screens.question: Tap every path with exactly two heads.

hints.text: Exactly two heads means exactly one tail. Where can the tail go?
Here is one such path. Find the others.

feedback.correct: HHT, HTH and THH: three of the eight paths.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Exactly two heads means one tail, in any of the three places.

byKey.h-h-h: HHH has three heads, not two. Exactly two means two and no more.
byKey.t-t-t: TTT has no heads at all.
byKey.h-h-t: You missed HHT. The tail can come last.
byKey.h-t-h: You missed HTH. The tail can come in the middle.
byKey.t-h-h: You missed THH. The tail can come first.
byKey.with-hhh: HHH has three heads, not two. Exactly two means two and no more.
byKey.one-path: HHT is one way to get two heads. The tail can also come first or second.

explain.text: Exactly two heads means one tail, and it can come first, second or third. So three of the eight paths qualify: THH, HTH and HHT.

screens.prose: The full list of possible results is the **sample space**, written $S$. For three tosses, $S$ has 8 outcomes, one per path. The paths you tapped form an **event**: a set of outcomes inside $S$.
screens.question: Which is the event “exactly two heads”, written as a set?

options.why: That holds one order only. The tail can sit in any of the three tosses.
2 is the number of heads, not an outcome. An event lists outcomes from $S$.
That is “at least two heads”. HHH has three heads, not two.

hints.text: An event lists outcomes, and each outcome is a whole path.
These are the paths you tapped.
Write each tapped path as three letters, inside curly brackets.

feedback.correct: Three outcomes, each a full path of three tosses.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List every path with exactly two heads, each as a full result.

explain.text: An event is a set of outcomes, so we list whole paths: $E = \{\text{HHT}, \text{HTH}, \text{THH}\}$. It sits inside $S$, which holds all 8 paths. We write $E \subseteq S$ and $|E| = 3$ for its size.

screens.prose: Same three tosses. Event $F$: the first and last tosses match.
screens.question: Tap every path in $F$.

hints.text: Look only at the first and third letters of each path.
HTH is in $F$: it starts and ends with H.
The first toss can be H or T, the middle anything, and the last must copy the first. That is $2 \times 2 = 4$ paths.

feedback.correct: HHH, HTH, THT and TTT: four of the eight paths.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep each path whose first and third letters agree.

byKey.only-heads: You kept only paths that start and end with H. Two tails match too.
byKey.all-same: You kept paths where all three tosses match. Only the first and last must agree; the middle is free.
byKey.h-h-t: HHT starts with H but ends with T.
byKey.h-t-t: HTT starts with H but ends with T.
byKey.t-h-h: THH starts with T but ends with H.
byKey.t-t-h: TTH starts with T but ends with H.
byKey.h-h-h: You missed HHH. It starts and ends with H.
byKey.h-t-h: You missed HTH. The middle toss can be anything.
byKey.t-h-t: You missed THT. The middle toss can be anything.
byKey.t-t-t: You missed TTT. It starts and ends with T.

explain.text: $F = \{\text{HHH}, \text{HTH}, \text{THT}, \text{TTT}\}$, so $|F| = 4$. The middle toss is free, so each choice of first toss gives two paths.

screens.prose: Back to the two dice. Event $B$: the red die shows more than the blue die.
screens.question: How many outcomes are in $B$?

hints.text: Go row by row. If red shows 4, which blue results are lower?
The cells below the diagonal have the red die higher.
Row 1 has 0 such cells, row 2 has 1, row 3 has 2, and so on: $0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells where the row number beats the column number.

byKey.ties: You included the doubles. On (3, 3) the red die does not show more.
byKey.half: Half of 36 assumes no ties. The 6 doubles sit in neither half.
byKey.differ: That counts every roll where the dice differ. In half of those the blue die is higher.

explain.text: The cells below the diagonal have red higher: $0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15$. The 6 doubles sit on the diagonal, and blue is higher in the other 15. Check: $15 + 6 + 15 = 36$.

screens.prose: Two more events for the dice. $C$: the total is 13. $D$: the total is at most 12. Each cell now shows its total.
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: $C$ is not an event, because it can never happen.
options.why: You dropped $C$ because it never happens. Any set of outcomes is an event, and the empty set is allowed.
13 is a total, not an outcome. No cell adds to 13, so $C$ holds no outcomes.

options.text: $C$ is the empty event $\varnothing$, and $D$ is the whole space $S$.
$D$ is not an event, because it always happens.
options.why: An event may hold every outcome. $D$ holds all 36 cells, so $D = S$.

hints.text: Find the largest total on the grid.
The largest total is 12, in one corner.
No cell reaches 13, and every cell is 12 or less. So $C$ holds 0 cells and $D$ holds all 36.

feedback.correct: $C$ holds no outcomes and $D$ holds all 36.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells in $C$ and in $D$, then name each set.

explain.text: No cell adds to 13, so $C = \varnothing$ and $P(C) = 0$. Every cell is at most 12, so $D = S$ and $P(D) = 1$. Both are events: the two extremes.

screens.prose: Sam lists two dice without caring which die is which: $\{1,1\}, \{1,2\}, \dots, \{6,6\}$. He gets 21 outcomes. Three of them total 7: $\{1,6\}$, $\{2,5\}$ and $\{3,4\}$.
screens.question: What is the chance of a total of 7?

options.why: You used Sam's list. It merges (3, 4) and (4, 3), which are different rolls.
You kept Sam's three pairs but used all 36 cells. Each pair has a mirror cell, so 7 has six cells.
You counted six cells for 7 but kept Sam's 21 below. Top and bottom must come from the same list.

hints.text: Is red 3 with blue 4 the same roll as red 4 with blue 3?
Sam's list hides these three cells.
Keep the dice apart: 36 cells, and 6 of them total 7.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the red and blue dice apart, then count.

byKey.sam: You used Sam's 21. His $\{3,4\}$ hides two different rolls, (3, 4) and (4, 3).

explain.text: Sam's $\{3,4\}$ covers two rolls, (3, 4) and (4, 3), but his $\{3,3\}$ covers one. So his 21 outcomes are not equally likely. Keep the dice apart: 6 of the 36 cells total 7, giving $\tfrac{1}{6}$.

screens.prose: Here is what you did. List every outcome once, keeping dice and tosses apart: that list is $S$. An event $E$ is any set of outcomes, from none to all: $$\varnothing \subseteq E \subseteq S.$$ Two dice give ordered pairs $(r, b)$, so $|S| = 6 \times 6 = 36$.
screens.question: Three dice: red, blue and green. How many outcomes are in $S$?

hints.text: Each outcome is a triple: red, blue, green.
Each die has 6 faces, and every combination is a different outcome.
$6 \times 6 \times 6$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the three dice apart and count every triple.

byKey.unordered: You ignored which die is which, as Sam did. Keep the dice apart: 6 choices for each.
byKey.added: You added 6 three times. Each red result pairs with every blue and green result, so multiply.
byKey.two-dice: That is two dice. The third die multiplies by 6 again.

explain.text: Each die has 6 faces, and every combination is one outcome: $6 \times 6 \times 6 = 216$. Merging orders, as Sam did, would give only 56, and those would not each be one roll.

screens.prose: A share trades at £50.00. Each day it moves up £1.00, stays flat, or moves down £1.00. We watch two days, so an outcome is a pair of moves.

state.caption: Start £50.00. U: up £1.00, F: flat, D: down £1.00.

screens.question: Shade every outcome where the share ends above £50.00.

hints.text: Add the two moves. Which pairs give a net rise?
Two up days, or one up day and one flat day.
Up, up ends at £52.00. Up, flat and flat, up end at £51.00. Every other outcome ends at £50.00 or below.

feedback.correct: Three of the nine outcomes end above £50.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two moves for each cell and keep the ones that end above £50.00.

byKey.only-uu: You missed up, flat and flat, up. One rise with no fall is enough.
byKey.one-order: You missed flat, up. It is a different path from up, flat, just like (4, 3) and (3, 4).
byKey.at-or-above: You included outcomes that end at exactly £50.00. Above means strictly more.
byKey.r1c3: Up then down ends at £50.00, not above it.
byKey.r3c1: Down then up ends at £50.00, not above it.
byKey.r2c2: Flat twice ends at £50.00, not above it.
byKey.r1c2: You missed up, flat. It ends at £51.00.
byKey.r2c1: You missed flat, up. It ends at £51.00.
byKey.r1c1: You missed up, up. It ends at £52.00.

explain.text: The sample space has $3 \times 3 = 9$ outcomes, one per pair of moves. Three end above £50.00: up, up and up, flat and flat, up. Up, flat and flat, up are different paths, just like (3, 4) and (4, 3).

ideas: The sample space $S$ lists every outcome once. Keep the dice, coins and days apart.
An event is a set of outcomes inside $S$. It can be empty, $\varnothing$, or all of $S$.
Order makes outcomes different: (3, 4) and (4, 3) are two rolls, so two dice give 36 outcomes, not 21.

formula.name: Sample space of two dice
formula.note: An event $E$ is a subset: $\varnothing \subseteq E \subseteq S$, and $|E|$ counts its outcomes.

summary.trap: Merging (3, 4) and (4, 3) gives 21 outcomes that are not equally likely. Counting them as equal gives wrong chances.

quiz.prose: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. One outcome is (H, 4).
quiz.question: How many outcomes are in the sample space?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pair each coin result with each die result.

byKey.added: You added 2 and 6. Each coin result pairs with all 6 die results, so multiply.
byKey.die: That is the die alone. Each face comes with H or with T.

explain.text: Each of H and T pairs with each of the 6 faces. So $|S| = 2 \times 6 = 12$, from (H, 1) to (T, 6).

quiz.prose: Two limit orders, A and B, are each filled (F) or not (N) by the close. An outcome lists A first, so FN means A filled and B did not.
quiz.question: Which set is the event “exactly one order fills”?

options.why: That is A filling alone. B can be the one that fills: NF.
That is “at least one fills”. FF has two fills.
1 is a count of fills, not an outcome. List the outcomes.

feedback.correct: FN and NF: one fill each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the outcomes with exactly one F.

explain.text: The sample space is $\{\text{FF}, \text{FN}, \text{NF}, \text{NN}\}$. Exactly one fill picks out FN and NF. Which order fills matters, so both belong.

quiz.prose: A price moves up, flat or down on each of two days. Ana lists the outcomes by net move: −2, −1, 0, +1 and +2.
quiz.question: How many outcomes does the full sample space hold?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. An outcome is a pair of moves, one for each day.

byKey.ana: You listed net moves, as Ana did. A net move of 0 comes from three different paths.
byKey.added: You added 3 and 3. Each first-day move pairs with each second-day move.

explain.text: An outcome is a pair of moves, so $|S| = 3 \times 3 = 9$. Ana's net move of 0 merges up then down, down then up, and flat twice. Her list loses paths, just as Sam's lost rolls.

quiz.prose: Two dice are rolled. Event $E$: both dice show an odd number, and the total is odd.
quiz.question: How many outcomes are in $E$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add two odd numbers and look at the total.

byKey.both-odd: Those 9 rolls have two odd dice, but every one has an even total.
byKey.odd-total: Those 18 rolls have an odd total, but each has one even die.

explain.text: Odd plus odd is always even. So no roll has two odd dice and an odd total, and $E = \varnothing$. The empty event is still an event, with $P(E) = 0$.
